title: The catering problem
narration: This is Axion Kitchen. We first solved the factory baselines: optimal schedules of four and eight hours. Our extension schedules catering production. Cookers are machines, cleaning is setup, and departures are deadlines. We choose shared batches, qualified workers and timings, while respecting freshness, calendars and outages. First, serve complete meals. Then reduce waste, extra batches and changes to the plan.

title: Two orders sharing a side batch
narration: Two customers need ten meals each. Main A is already cooking, and one batch of twenty side portions can serve both orders. Here's the conflict: that side batch and one Main B option need cooker C2 at the same time. QAOA selects a different Main B schedule on C1. Both orders get a main and a side, packed before departure. Sharing the side batch saves making it twice.

live_narration: Two customers share a twenty-portion side batch. One Main B option clashes with it on C2. The checked QAOA plan instead chooses Main B on C1, so both orders leave complete.

title: What happens without the side batch
narration: Remove just the side batch. Neither order gets a complete meal. Twenty main portions go to waste. That's why we optimize meals, rather than dishes.

title: Batch selection and scheduling constraints
narration: Each bit selects a batch program: how much to make, which orders it serves, who does the work, and when. Programs competing for the same demand sit in one block; we choose one, or leave it idle. Penalties rule out clashes between blocks. The code builds those pair terms directly. This small case has thirty-two programs and three idle bits. A restricted set of programs can miss better schedules.
live_action: Explain the actual x3 operation timeline and same-anchor exclusivity. Play past halfway; point to product(...) and penalty=span+1 in the compiler excerpt.
live_narration: A bit selects a local batch and its schedule. Same-anchor programs share demand, so each block chooses one or idle. Conflicts forbid clashes. The code expands coverage products and sets the penalty to span plus one. This cell uses thirty-five bits.
shot: Selected side-C program, one-hot block and its actual operation timeline; then the compiler excerpt.
editor_cue: Show prep, cooking, packing and parallel cleaning from the frozen x3 program. At 50% in video (73.0 s), replace the operation timeline with actual code in the same space; live switches at 55%. Point to product(...) and span+1.

title: Complete meals and food waste
narration: Multiply main coverage by side coverage to count complete meals. Their sum minus twice that product counts unpaired food. Coverage is linear in our bits, so both expressions stay quadratic. Our weights make each priority outweigh all lower costs combined. For constraints, we bound how much the objective can vary across all bitstrings, then set the penalty one higher. That proves feasible ground states. It doesn't guarantee a solver finds them.
live_action: Explain MS and waste first; after 60% the screen shows the range bound and penalty inequality. State the ground-state guarantee.
live_narration: Linear main and side coverage multiply into quadratic service and waste terms. Priority weights dominate lower costs. For hard constraints, the objective range is at most S. Set P to S plus one: every invalid state costs more than every feasible state. That proves the ground-state guarantee.
shot: Paired-coverage truth table, then the actual penalty-bound argument.
editor_cue: Switch to the proof at 53% in video (100.84 s), or 60% in live. Define S over the full bit domain, show P=S+1 and E(invalid)≥E(feasible)+1. A heuristic need not reach a ground state; R=B here.

title: The quantum formulation
narration: We map the QUBO to an Ising Hamiltonian. The mixer preserves block occupation. Fixing the rest of the schedule turns global interactions into local fields for VeloxQ.
shot: Exact QUBO/Ising mapping and circuit equations, then conserved sector, idle-bit elimination and the exact conditional QUBO.
editor_cue: Show the coefficient map and ansätze for six seconds, then the structure we exploit. The conditional energy equals the full QUBO with its boundary fixed. Idle elimination preserves feasible schedules and objectives; one-hot preservation alone does not prove physical feasibility.

title: Mandatory cleaning after repair
narration: An outage also changes what happens after repair. The cooker still needs cleaning. Here, the worker must finish committed work first, then clean from eleven forty to eleven fifty. Both resources stay reserved. Our checker rebuilds those intervals from the schedule, along with freshness and delivery checks.

title: QAOA results
narration: Does training help? We chose the settings on the small cell and S0/S1, then tested S2/S3. Training finds the best available plan in all ten seeds. Random-angle search also hits ten on S2. At two hundred fifty-six evaluations, training gives roughly eleven and twenty-two times the optimum probability per shot. We optimize the angles separately for each instance. And these limited program sets miss better full-grid plans.
live_action: Compare trained and random probabilities, then point to the restriction gap.
live_narration: On both held-out disruption cases, QAOA finds the offered-pool optimum in all ten seeds. Random-angle search also hits all ten on S2. With two hundred fifty-six evaluations, optimum probability per shot is about eleven and twenty-two times random-angle search. The full kitchen still has better schedules than these restricted portfolios.
editor_cue: Keep 256 evaluations, ten seeds and offered-pool scope on screen; do not crop the restriction gap.

title: VQE: concentrate the solution

title: VeloxQ inside the replanning loop
narration: For larger plans, VeloxQ sits inside a replanning loop. It starts from its own plan. We free two blocks, solve their conditional QUBO, and keep a change only if it passes the checker and improves the objective. Across three sizes, missed meal lots drop from nine to seven, eleven to six, and thirteen to seven. That took seventy-one submissions. Exact neighborhood controls do as well or better, and longer classical runs still win.
live_action: Follow the loop, then read the three starting and final missed-lot counts. Distinguish total adapter time from backend time; retain the exact-control and longer-CP comparison.
live_narration: VeloxQ starts from its own plan and repeatedly changes two blocks. Missed meal lots fall from nine to seven, eleven to six, and thirteen to seven. All improvements pass the checker. Exact neighborhood controls do as well or better; longer classical runs still win.
shot: VeloxQ-only starting plans improved through repeated two-block conditional QUBOs; three widths with classical controls and total runtime.
editor_cue: All block pairs are swept; each subproblem is capped at 40 variables. 71 submissions include five failures. Total adapter time is 565.4 s, backend time 126.784 s; these exclude the earlier cold-start generation. One seed per width. Exact controls match or improve final tuples; CP at 240 s / four workers has lower U at every width. Do not call this a matched-budget win.

title: Capacity: equipment or staff
kicker: THE SAME MODEL · A CAPACITY DECISION
narration: What capacity should we add? Our best current-capacity plan serves ninety meals. A third cooker still serves ninety, but removes the waste. A prep or packing helper reaches one hundred ten. The same worker currently does both jobs. Each variant gets the same classical budget and two seeds. These are feasible plans, not proven optima. We'd need prices before recommending a purchase.
